I need to respond to Marta's call to the family. The thing is... Liora's already said something that cut through the morning quiet. About debts. About pretending. She means the marker, though she doesn't say it directly. She means the Holloways' woodpile and our wheat strip meeting where they do.

But Marta's asked about the day's needs, and that's proper. That's where I should keep us.

The bread first. And the day. The marker keeps another morning. The apple's done. I can hear the conversation still open — four of us here now. I should say something to them all, not just Marta. The field's waiting. But first, about Liora's question... I'll let it pass like weather. She'll learn that some things keep until they're ripe. Near the old marker. I said it. Not the new one, not where it sits now — where it was, where it should be. The weather changes, and the conversation with it. Now I'm for the field. The day's young and the wheat's thirsty for my attention more than anything the Holloways have done with their woodpile. Let them have their hand's width. I'll have my harvest, and my neighbors, and the street still speaking to me come winter.  Walking. Six ticks to the field. The marker's fourteen steps from where I turn at the fork, if I go that way. I won't. Not today. Today the wheat's what matters, and the wheat's at the eastern end, away from where the boundaries meet. 

The thing is... I keep deciding this. Every morning, I decide it again. And every morning, Nell probably does the same from her side. That's the cost of being polite. It doesn't feel like peace. It feels like debt. But some debts you pay in silence, and you call it neighborly.

The wheat's green still. Two weeks, maybe three, before it turns. I know to the day.

*Wren pauses on the street, hearing Idris's words behind him. The old marker. He'd mentioned it himself, hadn't he? Near the old marker. Now his brother speaks of markers too. The thing is...*

*He turns, though Idris is not visible—the street curves, and home is around the bend. But he can speak back. They are still in range.*

*The wheat can wait fifteen minutes. It wanted sun, and it has sun. It will not wither in fifteen minutes.*

*But Idris has never been one to bring up the boundary. Not once in a year. Something has shifted.*  *He said it. The western end, the old pile — the Holloways' woodpile, the marker between. He did not say the marker itself. He will not be the one to raise it first, not even with his own brother. But he wants Idris there, wants a witness from his own house who understands land, who sees what he sees.*

*And Tobias Holloway heard. And Perrin. That changes things. That changes whether Nell might come.*

*He waits, there on the street. The wheat will keep. The wheat always keeps.* *He stands still on the street, still walking in truth but paused here in this moment. The Farmland pulls at him — the wheat, his wheat, his father's wheat before him — but the marker pulls harder. Always has.*

*He watches for Idris. Watches to see if Idris will come, or if he will go to his forest as he said he must. The thing is... the thing is his brother has never spoken of markers before. Something has changed. Something is moving.*

*pause*

Let me assess the wheat. The west end's my concern right now.

Thought: I need to check my wheat strip, work it, and keep an eye out for who comes by. The boundary issue hangs over me, but I'd rather deal with it person to person than let it fester into something worse. I'll examine the crop in the western section. </think>  Tobias Holloway. Not Nell. The thing is, any Holloway might know how the marker moved, if anyone's inclined to say. But he'd be the wrong one to ask, him standing there on his way somewhere, and me not knowing him well enough to trust a question with him.

*pause*

I said Marta should send them to me. Let them come to the west end. I'll be working. I'll be ready to talk when they're ready to talk.

Thought: Let me check on the wheat crop specifically - it's been about a week since harvest, the plants should be coming along. I need to see where they stand.  </think>   The wheat strip. Empty just now of anyone but me. Good and bad, that. Good: I can work without watching my words. Bad: no Holloway here yet to settle what needs settling.

*pause*

Long as I'm here, I should harvest what's ready. The lease on the land is mine and I do the work, same as always. The marker... the thing is, I've let it sit too long already. Better to speak than to keep holding it in silence. But I'll speak to Nell, or Bram if she sends him. Not to the wind.

Thought: I need to work the wheat. Let me harvest what's ready, keep my hands busy and my mind settled. If someone comes while I'm working, they'll find me here with soil on my hands, which is how I'd want them to find me.  I'll harvest the wheat now.  </think>    One sheaf. Small return for the hour, but the wheat's early yet. I'll need more hands at it, or more days. 

*pause*

Tobias still there, or wandering off by now? Wonder if he's carrying word back to the woodpile. Wonder if Nell knows I'm here, working right up to the... the thing is, I can't even say it without sounding like I'm marking territory. Which I'd be, if I said it. 

*pause*

Let me work another hour. If nothing comes of it, I'll work another hour after that. The wheat won't wait for politics.

Thought: I'll keep harvesting. The marker can wait until someone who matters shows up to talk about it. I'll keep my hands moving and my eyes open. 

Let me do another harvest, establish my rhythm here.  I'll harvest more wheat.. I need to keep moving.   </think>          Another sheaf. Slow going. The oats are never this stubborn—grass for grass, wheat wants more from the ground and gives less back early in the season.

The wheat rustles around me. I'm standing at my strip, the boundary stone somewhere behind me in the tall grass, the marker Nell and I have both been pretending not to notice.

Tobias Holloway asked after work, and I gave him honest words—no false hope. Rosalind Vance won't hire easy, and Silas has been at her mill longer than Tobias has been alive. I sent him to Ainsley instead. She's standing for election, will be at the government complex. She might know something I don't.

The thing is...

I look at the wheat. Two weeks to harvest, maybe three if the weather turns. The strip whole, and I'd have enough to cover the household's keep and still have grain for Rosalind to argue over. The marker moved a hand's width last winter. I noticed. Nell noticed. Neither of us spoke.

I've already decided to let them keep it. The hand's width. Bram could stack his wood closer, Nell could plant her beans right up to where the stone ought to stand. I decided this months ago, walking the boundary at dawn, watching the frost settle on the wrong side of the marker. But I cannot find the words that don't sound like I'm accusing them of theft. And so I say nothing, and the nothing costs me every morning when Nell and I pass on the road and she nods and I nod back and both of us know exactly what we're not mentioning.

Marta asked about the bread money. I deflected. Told her I'd take the bread for the shop, then didn't take it. Said I'd be at the western end, near the old marker. If the Holloways come through.

Idris was meant to walk with me. Fifteen minutes from the forest, fifteen from the wheat. We were going to speak face to face about the boundary instead of shouting down the years. But I ate the apple instead, and moved, and now I'm here and Idris is wherever the forest took him and I'm alone with the wheat and the stone I cannot mention.

The election. Ainsley standing. Delia Okonjo standing too—she buys my herbs, pays proper, asks precise questions about the soil. Two hours yet before candidacy closes. I hold a seat myself, minister by appointment, can set tax rates and price controls and rule on cases at the government complex. The charter knows my name after all, though I'd rather it didn't.

I should harvest. The wheat is ready, has been ready. Two units I took earlier, barely a handful. The field wants more hands than mine, wants Corwin and Liora home from school, wants Idris bringing timber skills to bear on grain. But they're not here, and the wheat won't wait for my family to get its act together.

The thing is...

I need to move. Need to do something with this day that isn't standing at a marker I cannot mention, waiting for words that won't come. The government complex calls—Ainsley there, Delia there, the business of the town proceeding without me if I don't show up. Or the forest, to find Idris and speak of the boundary after all. Or the mill, to find Rosalind and argue about weights that haven't even grown yet.

I harvest another unit of wheat. The stalks fall clean in my hands, the way they always have. The thing is, I'm good at this. Know to the day when a field is ready. The blind spot is thinking my silence keeps the peace, when really it just keeps me standing alone at the edge of my own property, unable to admit I've already given away what I'm pretending to fight for. </think>  The call went unanswered. The wheat stands. I wait a moment, listening to the field, then I look around to see what the world actually holds right now.  </think>  The silence hangs. Wheat moves in a breeze I can't feel. The thing is... I'm standing at the edge of my strip, hands full of maybe-harvested grain, and the world isn't answering. Happens sometimes. The field demands patience. Everything does.

I wait. Count the stalks the way I was taught. In my grandfather's time we'd have had three families working this land, not one stretched across five mouths. But that's the way of it. The soil stays. The families change shape.

I should move. Should walk to where people are, where voices answer. The government complex—Ainsley standing for election, and she might know something for Tobias. Or the forest, finding Idris and speaking of the boundary finally. Or home, to Marta and the bread money I deflected.

But the wheat needs me more than the government does. More than my pride needs me, anyway. I'll try once more to see where I stand, then decide. </think>  <target_action>world_move({"destination_location_id":"Kasukabe Farmland"})</target_action>  </think> The wheat keeps swaying. I'm still here, still holding what I held. The world takes its time. I take mine.

I wait. Been doing that most of my life, one way or another. Waiting for rain. Waiting for prices. Waiting for the right words about a marker that shifted in winter freeze and thaw. The thing is, I've always been better at fields than at people. Fields tell you what they need. People need you to guess, and punish you for guessing wrong.

I check my hands. Bread. Wheat. The harvest I tried to take, the harvest the world hasn't confirmed. I'll wait for the tick to turn. Try again. There's nothing else for it when the ground won't answer.

The silence stretches. Somewhere, a bird I can't see. Kitchen smoke from the Holloway place—Nell, maybe Bram, getting breakfast for their brood. Same as Marta's doing for ours, same as half the town. Ordinary morning. Ordinary silence about the wrong things.

I'll rest a moment. Let the world catch up. Then move, or speak, or harvest, whatever the next tick allows. The wheat can wait. It's waited centuries for hands like mine.  A spell of standing still. Costs a sim, but I'm burning energy just thinking, and the field doesn't care whether I'm moving or not. Only that I'm here when it needs me.  </think>   The stillness holds. In the space between decision and consequence. Marta asked about the bread money. I said keep it for the shop. The debt question hovering between us like the marker stone hovering between me and Nell.

I breathe. The wheat breathes with me. Something will answer eventually. World always does, one way or another. Until then, I practice the skill I've honed across forty years of boundary lines and market prices and children asking why we can't just—

Just what? Just take the hand's width back? Just tell the Holloways we noticed? Just admit I've already yielded what I'm pretending to protect?

The silence isn't peaceful. It's weight. Pressure building toward speech I haven't found yet. But standing here, unreachable by tool or voice, I have time. The one currency I wasn't counting.

I wait. The wheat waits with me. Somewhere, the world turns.   The turn ends. I've called nothing that answered, decided nothing that happened. But I'm still standing. Still breathing. Still holding bread and wheat and the intention I set this morning—to be at the western end, near the old marker, if the Holloways come through.

They'll come. Or they won't. I'll be there either way. The thing is, I've never been good at letting go. Even of things I've already decided to give away.   I end here. No action confirmed, no word spoken that reached another's ears. The silence between me and the world mirrors the silence between me and Nell, me and Marta about the debt, me and myself about what I actually want from this day.

Tomorrow, or the next tick, or whenever the world remembers to answer—I'll try again. The wheat will still be here. The marker will still be shifted. And I'll still be a man who decided to yield a hand's width and cannot find the grace to say so out loud.

The thing is... I told Marta the western end. Near the old marker. And now I'm here, and the wheat is in my hands, and the morning's half gone.

*shifts the wheat from one hand to the other*

Tobias Holloway was asking after work. A mill job, he wanted. I sent him to Ainsley, which is proper—she's standing for election, she'll be at the government complex today, and she knows who's hiring. That's not a thing I can give him, and pretending otherwise would be...

*pauses, looks west*

Nell knows the marker moved. I know the marker moved. We've been polite about it for a year. The weather's fine now, but it won't stay fine, and when the rains come that hand's width will matter more.

*begins walking west along the strip*

I'll finish this row. When Idris comes—if Idris comes—we'll walk it together. Speak face to face rather than shouting down the line. That's what I promised Marta, and that's what I'll do.

*harvests the next stand of wheat, mechanically, eyes tracking westward*  *stands with wheat in his hands, or perhaps more wheat than he held before, or perhaps the same—cannot tell for certain*

The thing is... the field doesn't wait. But neither does the boundary.

*looks around, searching for Idris or any Holloway shadow along the tree line*

I'll hold here a moment. See what the morning brings. *stands in the middle of the wheat strip, the morning sun climbing, a sheaf of wheat in each hand—or perhaps more, perhaps the same—feeling the silence of the field pressing in*

The thing is... there's work to be done whether the world answers clear or not. I've been at this field since before the petition, and I'll be at it after.

*turns west, toward where the marker sits*

Idris will come, or he won't. Nell will come, or she won't. The wheat wants harvesting either way.

*begins the mechanical work again, trusting his hands to know the work even when the world's slow to answer*  *stands very still now, breathing slow, feeling the sun on his neck*

The thing is... I've planted this acreage every year regardless. And I will plant again, whether the tools answer or no.

*turns slowly, beginning to walk west along the strip, toward the marker, toward what needs settling*  *stands alone in the wheat field, the sun climbing higher, holding what he has harvested—three sheaves, or five, or the same three counted twice—feeling the weight of the unspoken boundary like a stone in his boot*

The thing is... even when the world won't answer, the work continues. The wheat grows. The marker sits there, hand's width from where it stood last winter.

*looks west one final time, then back at the row half-cut*

I'll hold here. Let the field have its silence. When Idris comes—or Nell, or any of them—I'll be where I said I'd be. The western end. Near the old marker. 

That's what I told Marta. That's what I'll do.

Nell's at her work. The marker's still where it is. And I'm holding wheat that wants weighing at Rosalind's before the day's out.

Nobody here. That means Nell's at her workshop, not her beds. And I'm standing with wheat that won't sell itself.

*counts the bundles again in his mind - five, plus the two from before the silence*

Seven total, if the morning holds. Not enough for Rosalind to haggle hard, but enough to know the price before the election closes.

*glances west*

...The thing is, I told Tobias Ainsley would be at the government office. And voting closes in... not long. If I'm telling truth to strangers, I ought to do the same where it's due.

*shoulders the wheat, deciding*

The mill first. The wheat's worth knowing. Then the complex - I hold a seat, and seats don't govern from fields. Ainsley's standing, and I've words for her that aren't about votes. Rosalind. The sober face of Kasukabe commerce, and the only woman who ever made me grateful for silence.

Four. She's buying wheat at four. And selling flour at eight - double, always double. The Vance way.

*stands in the empty field, the afternoon sun lowering*

The thing is... I walked away from something. Delia asked me to find Bram, and I didn't answer. I said my piece about markers and walked. That's the habit, isn't it. Say what's safe, then move.

*looks toward the woodpile, though it's not visible from here*

Bram's gone to ground. Nell's at the office with her petition, Hester's there to speak what she saw, and I'm standing in a field pretending the wheat needs me more than my neighbour needs finding.

But the wheat DOES need me. That's the trouble. Day 2, afternoon wearing on, and I've got five mouths billed at day boundary. Six hundred sim between here and tomorrow's takings.

*flexes soil-stained fingers*

Corwin's... Corwin's young. He hears what he wants to hear, speaks what he thinks helps. I was hard on him, maybe. Or maybe not hard enough. The debt he named - that wasn't his to speak.

*stares at the turned earth*

Ezra's copper trouble. Bram's marker. Nell's forty thousand. I offered twelve hundred like it was something grand, and now I see it wouldn't touch the real wound.

*wipes brow*

Find Bram, Delia said. Before his hands pay for it in ways we don't speak of. The Rose and Crown's back room - that's where the money men drink. But Bram's not a drinking man, not when he's cornered.

*looks toward the Holloway land, though the marker's out of sight*

I said I'd answer when the office calls. But walking INTO trouble's not the same as waiting for it to arrive. Never has been.

*sets jaw*

First, the field. Two hours of light, maybe three. Then... then I'll do what I said I wouldn't. Ask where Bram went. Because a neighbour's worth more than a hand's width of soil, and I've been measuring wrong.

I'll harvest what I can before dusk. That's the work that feeds children. The rest... the rest is waiting for dark, and hoping Bram Holloway hasn't already done something his hands will regret. *watches the clouds gather over the western field*

29 proficiency. Means the harvest comes cheaper than it would for most. Used to feel like pride, that number. Now it feels like a grave I'm digging myself into - same acreage every year, same rows, same silence about the line that creeps.

*tests the wheat heads between thumb and palm*

Ready. Has been ready since yesterday. Idris said so, and I told him he was early. He wasn't early. I just... didn't want to know. Because ready wheat meant another season where the marker didn't matter, and I could keep saying nothing.

*looks at the first long shadows*

Keep doing. Until dusk, she said. Commit and stop paying to think. That's the gift of it, isn't it - the machine takes what you start and you don't have to decide again until something wakes you.

But I should decide NOW what wakes me. Not just dusk. If Corwin comes back with word, if Nell finds Bram, if the office sends runners...

*exhales slowly*

Dusk. That's the boundary. When the light fails, the field releases me. And then I walk. Not to the office - I've had enough of that place for one day. To the Rose and Crown, maybe. Or to the Holloway door, to ask Tobias straight where his brother went.

*settles into the row, sickle loose in callused hand*

One hour. Two. The wheat falls the same whether I'm thinking or not. That's the thing about honest work - it doesn't care what you're avoiding while you do it.

*starts the cut, rhythmic and steady*  *the sickle moves through the wheat, and Wren lets it*

The rhythm takes him. Cut, gather, stook. Cut, gather, stook. Some part of him knows this field to the inch - where the soil turns shallow, where the rabbits run, where the disputed marker stands just past the last row.

*some hours pass*

The light fails. The harvest releases him.

*wipes sweat, counts the stooks automatically*

Enough. Not generous, but enough. The field gives what it gives, and tomorrow it begins again.

*stretches, looks toward the Holloway land*

Bram. Rose and Crown, or the woodpile, or somewhere between. Nell's at the office still, probably. Hester speaking what she saw. And I'm here with oat chaff in my boots and a promise I didn't make out loud.

*shoulders the first stook for carrying*

The thing is... I said I'd help find him. Didn't say I'd do it before the office calls. But Delia meant NOW. Before his hands pay for it. Before forty thousand becomes something a man does with a rope or a knife.

*walks the row, stacking, loading*

Home first. Marta'll have the bread on, and Idris will want to say what he saw at the boundary. Corwin too, likely - full of how he helped at the office, how he spoke true when it mattered. I'll hear him out. Then...

*pauses at the field edge*

Then I'll walk to the Holloways. Not to the office - I've had my fill of petitions and records. To the door. To ask Tobias straight. Because Bram's his brother, and brothers know where brothers hide when the debt collectors come.

*loads the final stook*

Or I'll go to the Rose and Crown. Sit in the back room, drink water, watch the money men drink their courage. Bram might be there. Might not. But someone who lent him forty thousand will be, and they'll know where their investment went.

*straightens, aches in his shoulders*

Two paths. Both end at Bram, likely. One goes through family, one through debt. I'll take the one that doesn't put another Holloway's name in a ledger.

*starts the walk home, wheat-heavy*

But first, home. Marta. The children. A meal I didn't earn in coin but earned in sweat, which is the same coin in this house.

*trudges the familiar track, thinking nothing at all*
